_comment: Patterns that must NOT appear on public GitHub. Data only -- consumed by sweep_public.py.
Why this exists: on 2026-07-28 a public issue was opened titled
'EPIC: Funding pitch deck -- ...'. It was renamed and closed within hours, but GitHub
still served the ORIGINAL title to anyone, unauthenticated, through the issue timeline.
Editing a public issue does not un-publish it. Only deleting it does.
So the sweep checks renamed-event history too, not just current text. That is the check
that actually caught the one real leak; a scan of live text alone would have reported clean.
Every pattern is word-anchored. An unanchored scan is worse than useless here: it cries
wolf until people stop reading it. Measured false positives from the manual sweep that
these anchors exist to kill -- 'CI gates' (10x), 'SoC family', a 'relative' table column,
and '@lru_cache' read as a user tag.

patterns.note: Named funders. Deliberately NOT a bare \bGates\b -- that matched 10 CI/architecture 'gates' and nothing else.
The strategy itself, not the word 'grant' -- 'grants nobody anything' (a licence phrase) matched a naive pattern twice.
Qualified only. A bare \bfamily\b matched 'SoC family' and 'same family/listing style'; a bare \brelative\b matched a table column header.
The portfolio/P0 strategy. Public repos should carry the engineering story, not the funding vehicle behind it.

Tagging a stranger on a public repo pulls an uninvolved person into our thread -- happened once with an '@COO' tag that resolved to a real, unrelated GitHub user. Owner and Python decorators allowlisted. WARN because role names in prose are legitimate; a human reads the list.

_exempt_note: This file necessarily contains the patterns themselves. It lives in the repo, not on the issue tracker, so it is not swept -- but the exemption is recorded for whatever consumes this next.
